summary:
Connecticut sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, an assessment built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking finds the state's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

A 2022 shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is lawful in Connecticut was banned in the patient's home state. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state that has criminalised gender-affirming care.

State law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, in public and private employment, in governmental services and in the receipt of goods and services; gender identity and expression were added to the statute in 2011. The state hate-crime law covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties, consolidated and strengthened by legislation signed in June 2026 and effective 1 October 2026.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. No. 7006, a birth-certificate sex marker can be changed without surgery on a notarised affidavit from the applicant plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating that the person has received appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. That change replaced an earlier surgery requirement, which the Senate voted 32-3 to remove on 1 June 2015. Driver's licences and state identification can be changed on request, and birth certificates, IDs and licences offer M, F and X options.

Since 1 July 2018, people in Connecticut custody are treated consistent with their gender identity, including in strip searches and in access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, and in housing based on recognised gender.

The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all school premises. In April 2021 a federal judge dismissed the lawsuits seeking to block transgender female athletes from competing in Connecticut girls' high-school sports, leaving their eligibility intact.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned with immediate effect after signing in May 2017, following House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by Governor Ned Lamont and effective 1 October 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised with effect from 1971, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, having been lowered to 15 in 1975.
tangentialFactors:
The ranking's lowest tier is defined by criminal penalties for bathroom use by transgender people and by multi-year prison terms for providing care, which is the contrast against which Connecticut's placement is drawn. Sixteen states and the District of Columbia hold healthcare shield laws, covering 38 per cent of the transgender population aged 13 and over, while 32 states and five territories hold none; youth-care bans are tracked in the same dataset, some of them permanently blocked.

Connecticut's protections operate alongside a national framework that has moved in the opposite direction on passports, entry screening and federal facilities, so a visitor's exposure is split between the state layer and the national one.
localsOnly:
Residents changing a birth-certificate marker use the 2015 procedure: a notarised personal affidavit plus a notarised statement of appropriate clinical treatment from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist. Licence and state ID sex designations change on request, and the M, F and X options are available across birth certificates, IDs and licences.

For people in state custody, the 2018 policy governs strip searches, housing assignment and access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials according to recognised gender. Students are covered by the anti-bullying statute on all school premises, including online conduct. Workers are covered by the gender-identity and expression discrimination ban in both public and private employment.

Providers and patients resident in Connecticut rely on the 2022 shield law when care lawful in the state is prohibited where the patient came from. The strengthened hate-crime statute takes effect on 1 October 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
The June 2026 consolidation of the hate-crime law takes effect on 1 October 2026, so the operative penalty provisions before that date are the earlier ones.

A bill passed in June 2023 to reform the 1991 definition of sexual orientation in the state discrimination statute was pending governor action at the time of the source.

The July 2026 ranking is a rubric-based assessment of tracked bills rather than a record of enforcement or incidents, and it does not measure how the state's protections are applied in practice.

The inventory contains no Connecticut-specific count of anti-trans violence or killings, so no comparison against the state's general homicide rate can be made.
